# Exact endpoint bound with one unit and one fractional positive coefficient

For m>=1 an integer and 0<=p<=1, define

    P_m(p)=Pr(E_1+pE_2>=E_0+(p/m)Gamma(m)),

with all variables independent and all exponentials of mean one. Then

    P_m(p)>=P_m(1)
      = (m/(m+1))^m (5m+3)/(4(m+1)).                         (1)

This proves the complete k=1 subfamily of the fractional-positive
stationary patterns in `candidate 9dace055ddbb6578`.
It makes no assertion for k>=2, arbitrary simplex normals, or general OC.

## 1. Exact probability and endpoint values

Put A=(1+1/m)^(-m). For 0<p<1 the survival function of E_1+pE_2 at x>=0
is [e^(-x)-p e^(-x/p)]/(1-p). The two Laplace transforms of the
independent negative sum consequently give

    P_m(p)=N(p)/(1-p),
    N(p)=(1/2)(1+p/m)^(-m)-A p^2/(1+p).                       (2)

Indeed its Laplace transform at one is
(1/2)(1+p/m)^(-m), while at 1/p it is
[p/(1+p)](1+1/m)^(-m). This proves (2).

The same expression extends continuously to p=0 with P_m(0)=1/2.
At p=1, N(1)=0 and differentiation gives

    P_m(1)=-N'(1)=A[(m/(2(m+1)))+3/4]
                    =A(5m+3)/(4(m+1)).                     (3)

Continuity of the probabilities at both endpoints also follows by
coupling the same exponentials. The limiting comparison has no atom
at equality because the independent E_1 has a continuous law.

The endpoint in (3) is at most 1/2. For m>=2, retaining the first
three terms of the binomial theorem gives

    (1+1/m)^m>=2+(m-1)/(2m)
      =5/2-1/(2m)>=5/2-1/(m+1)=(5m+3)/(2(m+1)).

For m=1 the same claimed endpoint inequality is an equality,
checked directly. This proves P_m(0)>=P_m(1).

## 2. A single change of sign in the second derivative

Direct differentiation yields

    N''(p)=(m+1)/(2m)(1+p/m)^(-m-2)-2A/(1+p)^3.               (4)

For m>1, let R(p) be the ratio of the positive term to the positive
quantity being subtracted. Its logarithmic derivative is

    (log R)'=3/(1+p)-(m+2)/(m+p)
             =(m-1)(2-p)/[(1+p)(m+p)]>0                    (0<=p<=1).

Thus N'' can change sign at most once on [0,1], and only from negative
to positive. At p=1 the derivative equals

    N''(1)=A(m-1)/(4(m+1))>0.

It follows that either N is convex throughout the interval, or there
is a c in (0,1) such that N is concave on [0,c] and convex on [c,1].
An endpoint zero of N'' causes no difficulty. At m=1, (4) is
identically zero and (2) gives P_1(p)=1/2 throughout.

## 3. The endpoint comparison

Set Q(p)=N(p)-P_m(1)(1-p). By (3),

    Q(1)=Q'(1)=0,        Q(0)=1/2-P_m(1)>=0.

On the convex final interval from Section 2, Q lies above its tangent
line at one, which is identically zero. On any remaining initial
concave interval, Q lies above the chord joining its two nonnegative
endpoint values. Therefore Q>=0 on the entire interval. Dividing by
1-p>0 in its interior proves (1); endpoint continuity includes p=0,1.

All variables m and p remain in their full stated domains. The proof
uses a sign-change calculation, not finite sampling of p or an assumed
coefficient-merging rule.
